title: Equal Pay Smash: Tennis Levels the Court for Men and Women
summary:
For decades, female tennis players have fought for something simple: equal pay for equal work. Now, that fight is scoring a major victory. The Women's Tennis Association (WTA) announced that starting next year, all combined 1,000 events—the highest level of competition outside the Grand Slams—will award equal prize money to men and women.

Some tournaments, like Indian Wells, Miami, Madrid, and Beijing, already did this, along with all four Grand Slams. But the Italian Open, Canadian Open, and Cincinnati Open had not. In 2023, Italian Open organizers promised equal pay by 2025 but didn't follow through. Now they will.

"Achieving equal prize money across all combined WTA 1,000 tournaments is a major milestone for tennis," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo. She added it shows the WTA's "continued commitment to leading the sports industry in delivering our athletes competitive and financial equality" and is "a testament to the enduring nature of the founding vision of the WTA."

The WTA was formed in 1973, and equal pay has been a goal since then. The organization also announced changes to the calendar to give players more flexibility. Players ranked in the top 50 will now only have to play four WTA 500-level tournaments instead of six. They can also swap one WTA 1,000 result for a stronger 500 or 250 result.

"We have listened to player feedback on the demands of the calendar, and responded with a meaningful reduction in commitments," Camillo said. American world number three Jessica Pegula called the 2027 changes "an impactful step forward for players," adding that they give players "more ability to build our seasons around our own goals—competitively and personally." It's a win for fairness—and for players' health.
why_it_matters: Sport is one of the most visible places where kids learn what their work is worth, so a tour that finally pays women the same as men sends a message far beyond tennis — into future jobs, wages and how people judge who deserves what.

background_read: The Women's Tennis Association, or WTA, is the group that runs the main women's professional tennis tour; it was founded in 1973 with the help of the American star player Billie Jean King, who pushed for women to be taken seriously as athletes.

That same year, the US Open became the first of the four Grand Slams (the sport's biggest tournaments: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open) to pay men and women the same prize money — King had threatened to skip the event if it did not.
Wimbledon, the oldest and most famous tournament in tennis, did not catch up until 2007, which shows how long this fight has lasted.
The WTA 1,000 events are the highest level of competition outside the Grand Slams, so the money there is still a very big deal for the players' careers.
Valerie Camillo is the WTA's chair — the person who leads the organization's board — and Jessica Pegula is an American player who has ranked third in the world.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — players and fans of women's sport
perspectives.description: Women on the tour will now earn the same as men at the biggest non-Slam events, and the lighter schedule may help them avoid injuries and burnout.

The change covers only combined WTA 1,000 events; lower-level tournaments, sponsorship deals and TV coverage still lag far behind. Italian Open organizers already broke one promise in 2023, so players may doubt the deadlines.
Tennis has been the testing ground for equal pay since the 1970s, and change has usually come only after sustained pressure from players and their union rather than from tournaments volunteering it.
Attention now shifts to the smaller events below the 1,000 level and to how fairly players are treated across the whole season. If the combined events succeed, players will likely push for more.
